The Indian green frog Euphlyctis hexadactylus is a large dicroglossid species widely distributed across the Indian subcontinent, where it inhabits shallow freshwater wetlands and rice paddies. Upon hatching from their gelatinous egg masses at water temperatures of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the emerging larvae have a remarkably low mass, with hatchlings weighing approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams] at the moment of chorion rupture. This minute mass is consistent with a small egg diameter near 1 millimetre and reflects the energetic constraints of external fertilisation in a warm aquatic environment. The period from oviposition to eclosion was recorded as 10 days [ab = 10 days] at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], a relatively brief embryonic duration typical of tropical anurans that breed in temporary pools. Post-hatching, the yolk-sac larvae remain briefly endotrophic as they absorb their endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to active filter feeding. The lecithotrophic phase appears to be quite short in this species, and the tadpoles rapidly become exogenously feeding herbivores that graze on periphyton and suspended algae during their free-swimming larval period.

During the extended aquatic larval phase, E. hexadactylus tadpoles undergo considerable growth prior to the metamorphic climax. The wet weight at metamorphosis differs between sexes, with female froglets reaching 1.4 grams  upon completion of tail resorption and gill regression, while male froglets are slightly smaller at 1.2 grams . This post-metamorphic size dimorphism is established before the juvenile stage begins and suggests an early divergence in growth trajectories, likely linked to the energetic demands of later oogenesis in females. The terrestrial juveniles, often referred to as froglets, spend the following months foraging actively on insects and other small invertebrates in the damp vegetation surrounding their natal ponds. This period of somatic development is critical for building the body condition necessary to eventually fuel the onset of gonadal maturation. Field surveys of recently metamorphosed individuals indicate that the transition from an aquatic tadpole to a terrestrial juvenile represents a significant shift in both ecology and physiology, marked by the development of lungs and keratinised skin.

Sexual maturation in the Indian green frog is tightly linked to body size and environmental temperature. Under captive conditions maintained at 26 °C [T = 26 °C], female frogs reach puberty approximately 730 days following metamorphosis [tp = approximately 730 days following metamorphosis], a prolonged juvenile period that allows them to accumulate substantial somatic reserves. Males, housed under identical thermal regimes at 26 °C [T = 26 °C], also attain sexual maturity around 730 days after metamorphosis [tp = around 730 days after metamorphosis], reflecting a similar developmental timeline between the sexes despite their differences in ultimate body mass. This synchronised maturation schedule contrasts with the pattern observed in some smaller ranid species, where males typically mature earlier. The delay until puberty in E. hexadactylus is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritises reaching a large adult size before diverting resources toward gametogenesis. Gonadal recrudescence in both sexes follows closely after the attainment of this threshold size, and calling behaviour in males becomes conspicuous shortly thereafter during the monsoon breeding season.

Adult body size in Euphlyctis hexadactylus shows pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females achieving larger dimensions than males. The ultimate snout-vent length for females reaches 14.5 cm [Li = 14.5 cm], reflecting a body plan that can accommodate a large clutch volume within the coelomic cavity. Males attain a slightly smaller ultimate snout-vent length of 14.0 cm [Li = 14.0 cm], a size that still places them among the largest frogs in their genus. This dimorphism is even more striking when considering mass, as adult females can attain an ultimate wet weight of 296 grams [Wwi = 296 grams], whereas males plateau at a lighter 215 grams [Wwi = 215 grams]. The nearly 40% difference in mass between the sexes suggests strong fecundity selection operating on females, favouring the capacity to produce large clutches. Comparative data from congeneric species such as Euphlyctis cyanophlyctis indicate that these maximal sizes are near the upper end of the range for the genus. Measurements from museum specimen series confirm that these dimensions are achieved only after several years of steady post-metamorphic growth under favourable conditions.

Longevity and reproductive output in the Indian green frog reflect a life history adapted to the seasonal predictability of monsoon rainfall. The maximum lifespan of this species is approximately 14 years [am = approximately 14 years] when maintained at a constant 26 °C [T = 26 °C], a surprisingly long duration for a tropical anuran and one that permits multiple breeding seasons over a lifetime. Females produce approximately 2000 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 2000 eggs per clutch], laying a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year] during the rainy season. This reproductive strategy, in which a large batch of small eggs is deposited annually, is typical of dicroglossid frogs that exploit ephemeral water bodies. The annual timing of reproduction is synchronised with the onset of the southwest monsoon, ensuring that temporary ponds are available for larval development. The combination of high fecundity, moderate lifespan, and delayed maturation suggests a life history that balances the risks of stochastic pond desiccation against the benefits of iteroparity. Individuals that survive to reproduce across several years can contribute substantially to population recruitment.
